extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of American government / political science
extracted.subtask_description: Expository analysis of the constitutional roles, working practices, and political effects of the United States Senate, including its legislative, executive, and judicial functions and the institutional features that shape its behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of a closure rule / unlimited debate
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no general rule in the Senate limiting the length of a debate or of a speech; attempts to introduce closure were made historically but not adopted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The absence of a closure rule is of great political moment: it can prevent passage of measures (example: in 1890 it prevented passage of a bill placing Federal elections under Federal control). This institutional absence has allowed systematic obstruction (filibustering) to be used and gives minorities leverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of taking divisions and roll-call voting
rubrics_metrics.description: Divisions are taken by calling the names of senators alphabetically rather than by separating into lobbies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Constitution allows one-fifth of those present to demand that the Yeas and Nays be entered in the journal. Senators answer 'Aye' or 'No', may ask leave to abstain, and may be excused if paired with another senator who states the pairing when called.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive session secrecy and sanction for disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: When the Senate goes into executive session the galleries are cleared and doors closed; an obligation of secrecy is supposed to be enforced by potential expulsion of a senator who discloses confidential proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practically, punishment has rarely been inflicted; newspapers often manage to ascertain what occurs in secret session. Example: an incident where a Western newspaper published a secret session account, leading to sworn denials and no punishments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tension between secrecy and publicity for Senate business
rubrics_metrics.description: There are competing arguments: publicity is believed by some to make for purity, while others defend secrecy as supporting the Senate's power and dignity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Movements within the Senate have pushed against secrecy (particularly regarding confirmations). Some members who oppose secrecy argue it prevents abuses; others, including respectable members, argue secrecy preserves the dignity and effectiveness of deliberation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate's executive functions: treaties and confirmations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Senate's chief executive functions are the power of approving treaties and confirming nominations to office submitted by the President.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Through confirming or rejecting engagements with foreign powers the Senate secures general control over foreign policy; participation by the Senate in negotiations can reduce difficulties stemming from executive-only negotiation by signaling likely ratification and committing the ratifying body in advance.

rubrics_metrics.name: President's discretion and best practice in communicating with Senate
rubrics_metrics.description: The President may choose whether to communicate current negotiations to the Senate and take its advice or submit a completed treaty; the best policy is generally to keep leaders of the senatorial majority and the Foreign Relations Committee informed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keeping Senate leaders informed lets the President 'feel the pulse' of the Senate, foresee what it may sanction, and reduces secret influences; success depends on confidence in the Secretary of State and his tact in dealing with senators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of secret sessions for treaty consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Secret sessions let the whole Senate consider presidential despatches or negotiation details without publicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Important matters are sometimes first submitted to the Foreign Relations Committee and discussed in secret to avoid disadvantages of publicity. However, no secret can be long-kept and secrecy leaks can occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treaty ratification requirement and minority power
rubrics_metrics.description: For ratification a vote of two-thirds of the senators present is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This supermajority gives great power to a vexatious minority and increases the danger of sectional or electioneering obstruction. The Senate may amend or propose a treaty draft, though practice usually has the executive initiate treaties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of sectionalism and electioneering in foreign policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Senatorial control over treaty confirmation can enable groups of Senators from States with particular interests to defeat treaties for sectional or party advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When regional interests oppose a treaty, their senators can persuade colleagues that rejecting the treaty will help party prospects at home. The public's indifference to foreign affairs often allows such conduct with little penalty; the executive is easier to hold responsible than a legislative body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate confirmation as a check on presidential patronage (but imperfect)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Senate's confirmation power is intended to prevent the President from abusing appointments, but in practice its protection is incomplete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the same party controls both branches, appointments are often 'squared' for party interests; when opposed, the Senate may accept poor appointments to embarrass the President. The participation of the Senate tends to cause less friction and delay in practice than might be expected; cabinet appointments are commonly confirmed as a matter of course, diplomatic officers rarely rejected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public discussion of nominations vs secret executive session
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an argument that nominations ought to be discussed publicly rather than in secret executive session.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A European observer's surprise that important business is transacted with closed doors has been echoed by senators advocating for more public discussion of nominations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate's judicial function in impeachment trials
rubrics_metrics.description: The Senate sits as a High Court for trial of persons impeached by the House; senators are 'on oath or affirmation,' and conviction requires a two-thirds vote of those present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method, though rarely used, is preferable where a political element exists rather than exposing the Supreme Court to such cases. Examples and statistics: eight persons have been impeached (including six federal judges with mixed outcomes).

rubrics_metrics.name: The Federalist's five aims for the Senate
rubrics_metrics.description: Hamilton set out five aims for creating the Senate: equal representation for States; a council to advise/check the President on appointments/treaties; to restrain the impetuosity of the House; to provide stability through experience and longer terms; to serve as a proper Court for impeachment trials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All five objects have been more or less perfectly attained and help explain the Senate's role as a 'centre of gravity' in government — checking both House and President and supplying stability over activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small size as a contributor to Senate effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: The Senate's small size educates members better than a large body: each member masters more of the business and feels the significance of his personal action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A small assembly mitigates abuse of free debate, fosters closer acquaintance among members that restrains posing and excesses, and leads to better habits in discussing and transacting business; historically the Senate began very small and retained these advantages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative permanence (six-year terms) promoting independence and expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Longer terms (six years) compared to the House's two years give senators opportunity to learn duties thoroughly and be more independent of immediate popular pressures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permanence and longer terms increase stability, improve training, and slightly reduce constituency influence — seen as a clear gain in the American context where politicians often chase passing public opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attraction and selection of superior talent to the Senate
rubrics_metrics.description: The Senate attracts the ablest and most ambitious men, giving it superior intellectual quality compared to the House.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons include greater power, dignity, longer service, and independence; natural selection brings higher average capacity, and years of service in a small body with executive responsibilities create political efficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior public experience as normative for senators
rubrics_metrics.description: Many senators have prior service in the House, state legislatures, as judges or governors — substantial public experience is typical and expected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statistics cited (e.g., composition of 61st and 62nd Congresses) illustrate that senators commonly have considerable prior public office experience, which contributes to their competence but may also instill habits of local politics and intrigue.
